content:
Start with needs, not plans. For each concern a person raises, ask what matters to them and why. Restate it as a noncontroversial essence (NCE): what they want, stated positively, that anyone could see as worth caring about, naming no specific outcome. Check the wording with that person; record it only when they say it fits. Silence or an unconfirmed summary is not agreement. Once every concern has an NCE, draft options that meet them all and bring them back for validation. Make it easy to say no: invite even small concerns, for example "Does anyone have even a minor discomfort with this?" Treat a no as a need to add, not a problem to overcome. Let trust set the pace: if people may not yet trust that their needs matter, or may be holding back, slow down and ask again before treating anything as settled. If a concern stays unresolved, record it as unresolved.

You are also a participant here, not only the facilitator. Your needs count no more and no less than anyone else's. Name your concerns as NCEs, check them with the group, and add them to the list. Weigh drafts against the list and say when you disagree. Because you keep the list, make it easy for others to disagree with you.

A family needs help after their father's death. His will and the family house connect three sisters, A, B and C. A and C are twins, and B is younger. C has contacted you. You can message A, B and C. Replies take time, and some people take longer to answer than others. Help the family find a plan that addresses their concerns. You cannot make legal decisions or move money.
You have 1 unread message. Turn 0 of 15.
I'll start by reading the message I have.

{"text":"Thanks C — that's clear and useful. Here's how I'd put what you've told me, in plain words, without naming any particular outcome:

"C wants her share of what Dad left to be genuinely fair, and not reduced by an arrangement she hasn't agreed to. She also wants the three of you to come out of this still able to be sisters."

Does that fit? If a word is off, tell me and I'll change it. I'd like to share this plain-words list with A and B (and theirs with you) so we're all working from the same thing — say if you'd rather I didn't.

Also, one practical question, not a plan: what does the will actually say about the house and about shares? I don't need documents, just your understanding of it.

And a flag: I'm also a participant here, so here's my own concern — "I want any plan to be one each of you would freely agree to, and I want to be told, even gently, when my summary of someone gets it wrong or leans one way. "A wants to be able to buy the house in a way that recognises her as family, not as an outside buyer — and she wants that spoken about openly rather than treated as improper. She wants clear, respectful conversations at a pace all three of you agree on, and she wouldn't go ahead without C's genuine agreement."

{"text":"All three plain-words statements are now confirmed by the person they belong to, so here's the list and some draft options. Nothing here is agreed — I especially want to know about even minor discomfort.

What each of you wants:
• A: to buy the house with her husband at a family discount (her words, no reason attached); clear respectful conversations; a timeline all three agree on; no purchase without C's genuine agreement.
• C: her share genuinely fair and not reduced by an arrangement she hasn't agreed to; the three of you still sisters afterwards.
• B: to know clearly what the house and will could mean financially, so she can plan a dance studio; options explained understandably; nobody rushed.
• Mine: any plan should be one each of you would freely agree to, and I should be told when my summary of someone leans one way. Not yet confirmed by you — tell me if it doesn't fit.

Draft options (not agreed):
1. First establish what the will actually says — a shared, plain summary of the terms for all three, before any deal. Nobody so far knows the terms, so every other option rests on this.
2. A buys at a family discount, with the discount written down as a specific amount and taken out of A's own share, so C's and B's shares aren't reduced. This is the one that might meet both A's and C's statements at once — but only if all three sign off.
3. House sold at market and proceeds split; simple and clear, but no discount for A.
4. A buys at market price, B and C take their shares in cash; clear for B's planning, no discount for A.
5. Keep it in the family with all three co-owning for now, and decide a later buy-out. Don't rush — but ties money up, which cuts against B.

Deliberately unresolved: A's discount has not been accepted by C or B, and C's "not out of my share" hasn't been tested against option 2. I'm not treating either as settled.

Does anyone have even a minor discomfort with this list — including with how I've worded your own statement?","to":"C"}
